speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Chairman, I beg to move, “That the total sum to be allocated for Head N of the Estimates be reduced by $100”.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: COVID-19 has brought about tensions in foreign relations amongst various nations.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Borders were hurriedly closed as governments attempted to stem the spread of the virus, and added to this was the tension arising from even the transnational supply of medical equipment.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Nationalism was rearing its ugly face and multilateralism was elbowed aside.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this pandemic the absence of cooperation is somewhat puzzling because global public health generally requires cooperation to control its spread and to minimise the damage to the global economy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Dr Joshua Busby of the Robert S Strauss Center for International Security and Law pointed out that, in the past, if we looked at various diseases and epidemics, the US and the Soviet Union found it within their interests to cooperate – and even outdo each other – such as on the eradication of smallpox in the midst of the Cold War.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The dissonance among leading nations, amidst this pandemic, prompted even Pope Francis last October to issue an encyclical, to lament the poor cooperation amongst countries and to warn that the forces of “myopic, extremist, resentful and aggressive nationalism are on the rise”.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I quote from that encyclical: “Aside from the different ways that various countries responded to the crisis, their inability to work together has become quite evident.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For all our hyper-connectivity, we are witnessing a fragmentation that made it more difficult to resolve problems that affect all of us.” With the then US administration vigorously advancing its America First policy, a mixture of nationalism, unilateralism and xenophobia, and its rivalry with China, the world was left, perhaps, with a leadership vacuum.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The resultant fallout was a relative decline in multilateralism and the weaponisation of global interdependence.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I recall that in the early days of the crisis, the great uncertainty that permeated as borders started closing and the then unknown virus was spreading rapidly.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I also remember many a frantic resident contacting to ask for advice as they or their family members tried to leave parts of the world, such as China, to return home for safety.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our MFA consular officers were tested up to the hilt to mobilise resources to bring Singaporeans overseas home to their families during this crisis.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A debt of gratitude to all those who worked so tirelessly then and now to bring them home.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These border closures also disrupted much of our supply chain.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, as a small nation, we have to work harder to protect our sovereignty and independence, and avoid being dominated by bigger countries.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To secure our place in the world, we need support and cooperation from other friendly nations who are also committed to an open rules-based global order and multilateralism.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There are many common threats which we can only overcome by working together with our allies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These challenges include climate change, pandemics, terrorism, cyberattacks, water shortage, food insecurity, just to name a few.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We are also dependent on partnerships for trade and other exchanges vital to our survival.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, we have put in much effort over the years to build strong and productive relationships with our neighbours and nations further ashore.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have been actively engaged with the international community and contribute to common goals.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In many areas, we are punching above our weight.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have established a track record as a fair, reliable and valuable partner.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Amidst the global uncertainty and growing geopolitical tensions, we need to re-strategise.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What are some of the practical measures that we have taken to maintain or strengthen Singapore’s reputation as a constructive and responsible member of the international community?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, Sir, for decades, Singapore has managed a free market economy and is well-positioned as an international and regional hub.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Would the Minister for Foreign Affairs share how will Singapore maintain its status as a hub for trade, shipping and finance given the economic uncertainties caused by this pandemic and what is our strategy to emerge stronger should the inflow of resources and talents be constrained by the pandemic?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, it is likely that the path to recovery will be long-drawn, uncertain and uneven in a post-COVID-19 world.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As mentioned in one of my earlier speeches in Parliament, I strongly feel that there is a need for Singapore to have a deeper cultural understanding of our ASEAN region, in view of greater potential growth opportunities, especially since ASEAN forms a strong economic powerhouse.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This greater interconnectedness is necessary, especially with the growing uncertainties and instabilities, such as rising protectionism over supply chains, resources, data and technology, as well as extraordinary levels of public debt globally to fund the exceptional financial responses during this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To achieve this, I propose that the Continuing Education and Training (CET) as well as SkillsFuture components for each ITM include understanding industry models, the supply chains, the business strategies and the cultural context of how things are done in our neighbouring countries.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These cultural knowledges developed through CET are essential for fostering people-to-people connections within the ASEAN region and to ensure stable business partnerships.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: COVID-19 has underscored the importance of Singapore towards strengthening its adaptability and resilience to cope with uncertainties and instabilities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As such, how may MFA assist to provide these opportunities within CET and SkillsFuture to support pre- and post-tertiary education and lifelong learning?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How may MFA strengthen our resilience via relationships, partnerships and people-to-people connections with other countries?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Chairman, Sir, in June 2020, Foreign Minister Dr Vivian Balakrishnan spoke in a virtual townhall with our Foreign Service officers and, within the excerpts of the speech published in The Straits Times, Minister Vivian highlighted that “finding relevance remains an existential imperative for us”.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: During a pandemic, “No one is safe until everyone is safe”.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But over the past year, we witnessed how some advanced economies were absorbed in their fight against COVID-19 with multiple lockdowns, or were embroiled in factious politics, leaving little capacity to fulfil their global role as they should.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Given the lack of global leadership, each of us then must try and do our best to help combat the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Despite the challenges and, small as we may be, Singapore must still do our part, to be helpful, relevant and be a responsible global citizen.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A Chinese idiom comes to mind – “雪中送炭”, which literally means delivering charcoal when snowing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is always tougher to give help to others when we are not having it easy, too.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But it is during tough times that we show our mettle and demonstrate genuine friendship.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, I would like to ask how is Singapore contributing to the international effort in combatting COVID-19 and how might our Singapore response evolve looking ahead?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In contrast, Singapore has endorsed the elevated stance that advocates for fair and equitable access for vaccines, or one of vaccine multilateralism.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Vaccine multilateralism is simply pragmatically necessary if international borders are to reopen.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, Singapore has been an active participant in various global initiatives.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have some questions on our contributions to these efforts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One of the key initiatives is the COVAX Facility, a global risk sharing mechanism aimed at equitable access to COVID-19 vaccines.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: More than 190 countries are now involved in COVAX.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the conditions of our donation, World Health Organization (WHO) Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus noted recently that the WHO could accommodate requests from governments that wish to earmark some of their donations to specific countries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Singapore is also serving as a co-chair of the friends of COVAX Facility alongside Switzerland.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could the Minister elaborate on what Singapore's role is as the co-chair and the actions plan by the grouping to assist the COVAX Facility?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Chairman, the COVID-19 pandemic is the crisis of our generation.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The impact on the lives and livelihoods of people around the world had been devastating.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In Singapore, we suffered the worst economic recession in our history.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: COVID-19 vaccines have been identified as the only long-term solution to counter the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We can then look forward to resuming even more activities.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, we are all keenly aware that our economy is highly dependent on broader economic developments beyond our shores.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a global hub, we need open borders between nations and the freedom to travel in order to thrive.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our survival requires continued engagement with other countries through trade and many other areas of cooperation and exchanges.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Thus, it is important for our economic recovery that everyone in the world, not just Singaporeans, has access to safe and efficacious vaccines.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is because no one is safe until everyone is safe in this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The threat of this evolving disease requires international cooperation and as some had described it, vaccine multilateralism.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will the Minister share with us details and updates on how Singapore is helping to promote vaccine access to the wider international community?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As one of the contributors to the COVID-19 Vaccine Global Access (COVAX) Advance Market Commitment (AMC) mechanism, what are our roles and contributions to the international effort?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Six members of ASEAN are among the countries eligible for COVAX assistance.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a member of ASEAN, what more can we do to help our closest neighbours?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How can we work with their leadership to ensure that the vaccines can also reach their needy, especially those in zones of conflict and unrest?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition to monetary contributions, will Singapore be deploying manpower or other resources to help?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Beyond our region, is there a role for us to assist in areas further afield, to lend a helping hand to our other allies?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Minister provide an update on these initiatives?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Mr Chairman, across the world, in the past one year, we have seen how cooperation is needed to solve many large and complex problems, distinguished by three key facets of modern life – porosity across borders, movement and mobility and high inequality.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is a mirror to the challenges that we face in climate change.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: They affect everyone and financial strength offers no protection because we are all in this together.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Like the virus, environmental pollution is no respecter of national borders.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There is no apportioning of blame because we are all users.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So how is Singapore collaborating with partners to maintain the positive momentum on climate change?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Mr Chairman, after a year of fighting COVID-19, much resources have been committed to stopping the spread of the virus.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: There is much toll in the economic, social, emotional aspects and no effort was spared galvanising the nation, saving communities and helping those who were most affected.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Given these immense challenges, will there be sufficient capacity for the greater challenge that remains – climate change and our existential need to achieve sustainability?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The warming of the earth over the next decade is unavoidable.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Many other planetary limits have been breached and we are on the verge of a tipping point where the loss of biodiversity, degradation of water, air and cooling systems of the world will be irreversible.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Mitigating climate change through decarbonisation is a key and necessary response.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: However, this was based on a growth and temperature rise estimates that have since exceeded assumptions.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I understand that despite all challenges, Singapore pressed ahead to submit its nationally determined contribution and long-term low emissions development strategy.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Could the Minister for Foreign Affairs provide an update on how will Singapore continue to contribute to the global efforts against climate change?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, in recent years, we see countries behaving in an insular manner.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Protectionism is on the rise as well as nationalistic sentiments.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Now, the pandemic also undermine international bodies for the alleged biases, leanings and political pressures.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, Singapore still needs to open up, work together with other nations through the various multilateral platforms.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Now, besides the pandemic, can the Ministry shine some light on what are the other important challenges facing Singapore that we are working with the international community and at multilateral platforms?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I would also like to take this chance to thank our MFA officers, especially those based overseas, who put in their lives on the line for the past one year, to defend Singapore's diplomatic interests and to assist Singaporeans overseas who are in need.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, even as relations between the US and China remain uncertain, Singapore is in a sweet spot and we are happy where we are.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Nowadays, wars are not fought with guns, but with market access, economic protection and the movement of people.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Naturally, the effects of these tensions are felt intimately by our SME towkays here in Singapore and they will definitely be watching how US-China tensions unfold.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is our hope that our neutral stance will continue to find resolve in the midst of these tensions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Mr Chairman, can I take my two cuts together?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: What I meant is, I can continue with the following cut?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Yes, you can take both cuts together as Mr Vikram Nair is not here.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Mr Chairman, Foreign Minister Dr Vivian Balakrishnan recently responded to questions on the situation in Myanmar.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: He stated that an escalation of the situation will have serious consequences for both Myanmar and the region.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Indeed, reports that developments remain highly fluid contrary to hopes for greater stability.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Dr Balakrishnan, in his earlier responses, has indicated a need for consensus to hold an ASEAN Foreign Ministers' Meeting on the Myanmar situation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: ASEAN's ability demonstrate initiative on the Myanmar issue may be key.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: We speak repeatedly about ASEAN unity and centrality but that centrality only matters if it is meaningful and can make a difference.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: This is important because an effective ASEAN helps members like Singapore maintain our autonomy and a platform to make our voices heard.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: So, it is imperative for the Government to bring Singaporeans on board with what it is doing to support our ASEAN's ability to play a practical and positive role when faced with unfolding situation in Myanmar.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Political instability in the region, even away from Singapore, can have an impact for us here.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Further, Southeast Asia is also a focal point or intensifying competition between the US and China, and any inability ASEAN to address such an ability could spur further contestation among major powers in our region.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: This may possibly cause severe and even irreversible divisions in ASEAN in ways that paralleled the recent crisis within the Pacific Islands forum.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Our Government's views, notwithstanding, perceptions in Myanmar and elsewhere in the world may differ.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Being in a position to extend support may be especially critical in the event of a further escalation of violence and instability.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Singapore's foreign policy towards the US and China has been one where we have reiterated that we do not wish to choose sides and want to retain the ability to make choices for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Our Prime Minister has even implored both Beijing and Washington to stabilise the US-China relationship and focus on building constructive ties.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: This position rests on the view that many areas of significant overlap in interest exists between the US and China, and will continue to exist if not expend.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: But this does seem at odds with recent global developments.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Mr Chairman, I think it is clear that the world has entered a new phase of renewed major power rivalry between the US and China.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Many are now familiar with US President Joe Biden's foreseeing extreme competition in US-China relations and General Secretary Xi Jinping's framing of a wide range of issues as PRC's core interests that the US should respect.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: A recent South China Morning Post editorial even noted that disputes between China and the US appear unavoidable.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Realistically, no amount of pleading or reasoning from Singapore is ultimately going to change minds in either Washington or Beijing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Any believe that a Kumbaya moment will come at any time soon, may be optimistic, but potentially naive.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: As a smaller actor, Singapore will probably do well to be prepared for the worst that may yet to come.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Given the current trajectory in US-China relations and the very real possibility of a more tense environment, several key questions loom large with Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: First, I would like to ask, how Singapore's autonomy and freedom of action can be protected under the more contentious circumstances that we find ourselves in today?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Second, how will Singapore maintain positive and robust ties with the two majors, competing against one another without getting drawn unnecessarily into the friction and risk being ground up in the process?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Third, how does Singapore avoid one party perceiving our efforts to stand for our own interests as being detrimental to theirs, and earning suspicion for siding with their rival?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I am asking these questions because Singaporeans need to understand and by into the Government's strategic vision on these aspects of our foreign and even security policies and the guiding principles there too, for us to have any chance at success in navigating these very tricky waters.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Chairman, may I have permission to take both my cuts together?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Singapore shares strong ties with Malaysia beyond economic, defence and trade to our people-to-people interactions and social relations.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Our interdependencies in the areas of jobs, food and water supply, transport links, tourism and trade, have only been further magnified in the last year from border restrictions arising from the pandemic.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: There are two concerns I would like to raise.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Since the Movement Control Order in March and the suspension of the Reciprocal Green Lane, movement has been reduced to travel under the PCA and commercial vehicles.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: This has a multi-fold impact on trade, tourism and also social ties between Singaporeans and Malaysians with family members across the border.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: With the roll out of the vaccination programs in Johor and Singapore, I would like to ask the Ministry if there are upcoming plans to reopen borders with Johor?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: The second is the high-level interactions with Malaysia.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Regular and active exchange of visits between our political leaders have, in the past, helped our leadership on both sides develop relations and better understand each other.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: These exchanges are important to set the tone and overall direction for our bilateral relationships.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: The COVID-19 pandemic and border restrictions have effectively put a halt to these physical interactions.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: How have these impacted our high-level interactions with Malaysia?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: We have a deep and multi-faceted relationship that is rooted in mutually beneficial cooperation across multiple sectors.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Similarly, our regular physical exchanges have been disrupted by COVID-19.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: It is essential that we maintain the close linkages between Singapore and Indonesia, so that we are ready to emerge stronger from the pandemic, which has impacted both our economies.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: It is encouraging to know we continue to collaborate on key economic projects such as the Industry 4.0 Programme.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: How will our two nations work together to overcome the challenges posed by COVID-19, and maintain essential connections and economic links?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, Singapore, Malaysia and Brunei are interlinked across social, economic, political, and security fronts.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore and Malaysia share a close relationship where many of our citizens live and work in both countries.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Prior to the pandemic, more than 300,000 travellers crossed the Causeway every day.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Despite the pandemic, bilateral cooperation between the governments of Singapore and Malaysia has resulted in the formation of the Reciprocal Green Lane (RGL) and Periodic Commuting Arrangement (PCA) travel schemes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, given the resurgence of COVID-19 cases in Malaysia, Singapore has suspended the RGL for a period of three months, beginning from February 2021.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Given the disruptions to cross-border flows, could MFA explain how we have maintained our close linkages?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Brunei is another close neighbour with whom we share a special relationship.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore and Brunei have long-standing arrangements such as the Currency Interchangeability Agreement and also cooperate extensively in defence, finance, trade and investment.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In April 2020, a joint ministerial statement released by nine countries, including Singapore and Brunei, affirmed commitment to ensuring supply chain connectivity, to facilitate the flow of goods including essential supplies, amidst COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In September 2020, Singapore and Brunei initiated a RGL to facilitate essential business and official travel for residents from both countries.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, Indonesia is one of our closest neighbours and our relations have been underpinned by family ties between the people of both nations, cultural exchanges, interdependence and substantive collaboration across multiple domains.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singaporeans and Indonesians travel between both countries frequently, to visit relatives and friends, for leisure, for study, work and business.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our ties run deep and go back a very long way.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The on-going COVID-19 pandemic has resulted in travel restrictions and caused much hardship for people on both sides.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is much harder now to do everything, whether it is seeing loved ones or continuing cross-border business projects.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How have we maintained or deepened this relationship during this challenging period?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What are some of the initiatives and projects to keep our relations strong?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, I would like to ask the Minister for an update about Singapore companies in Sub-Saharan Africa.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Minister provide an update on how our companies are tapping this growing market and which sectors they are developing?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While it is less familiar to most Singaporeans, it is an emerging market with great potential.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Due to its young population, Sub-Saharan Africa is growing quickly and presents many opportunities which will do us well to seize them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I understand that Singapore is one of the larger investors in Africa among Southeast Asian countries.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As of 2019, there were more than 60 Singapore companies operating there.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They covered a wide range of sectors, including agribusiness, manufacturing, logistics and digital services.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How has our trade with them been progressing and would the Minister share some details about our investment figures and market share?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How else is the Ministry supporting Singaporeans working and doing business there, especially in this COVID-19 environment?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Despite the devastation from COVID-19 last year, ASEAN was able to adapt.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The signing of the RCEP serves to broaden and deepen ASEAN's engagement with Australia, China, Japan, Korea and New Zealand.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: At the same time, there are also fault lines which could unravel and undo all the progress ASEAN has achieved to date.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: These fault lines play on the differences between ASEAN member states.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: A recent survey entitled State of Southeast Asia 2021, was conducted by the Yusof Ishak Institute of Southeast Asian Studies, among more than 1,000 academics, policy-makers, business people, civil society leaders, media and other organisations, from the 10 ASEAN member states.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Recent happenings in Myanmar are highly regressive from a human rights perspective.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: ASEAN's operating principle of working through consensus, may be seen as a stumbling block at such times.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Given the above, I would like to ask the Minister for Foreign Affairs on how Singapore will seek to strengthen ASEAN's centrality and coordination?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: How will we work further through the ASEAN economic community and the ASEAN political security community?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: What about the potential of NGOs and the people to strengthen ASEAN?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He also signalled that Singapore must deepen its capacity to collaborate and innovate with partners around the world, especially the ASEAN countries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It may seem incredible, but over the course of the past one year, where all eyes appear to be focused on the Herculean effort in healthcare, social compliance and understanding the virus itself, two things happened under the radar, which shows that we have kept faith with the vision and how it stood us in good stead.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, the securing of sufficient supply of vaccines ahead of other countries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And today, Singapore is in a very good position to emerge from the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We must not take for granted that a small country with no bargaining power can secure a reliable supply of such a precious commodity and provide logistics, not just for Singapore, but for others in the region.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We have heard of expansion of global firms in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We are therefore in a good position to realise the ambitions of a Global-Asia node.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The question arises as to how MFA can facilitate these ambitions?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How does MFA's work to enhance cooperation with these countries contribute to this imperative?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The first is in the area of setting standards.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, the area of human capital development, and the third, international business linkages.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: All these rely on innovation, enterprise and technology.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These must not be the esoteric domain of glass and steel in biopolis, but must flow into the conversations of coffeeshops in our housing estates, into "what I want to be when I grow up" essays in primary schools.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Global-Asia node cannot be an ambition for the few, but a lived reality for all.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Can the Minister tell us how MFA's efforts to make Singapore as a global Asia hub, improve the daily lives of Singaporeans, especially during these difficult times?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Chairman, Singapore has always been strongly committed to free trade and connectivity as this is the foundation of how we make a living as a nation.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister share how will Singapore be supporting ASEAN, especially this year's Chair, Brunei, to forge a closer ASEAN for the benefit of all?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore has and will continue to thrive because of our openness to connect to all our partners around the world.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We are friends with every country of the world and I believe we will and must continue to be so.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: While we should press on with such efforts in our neighbourhood, this pandemic has also shown the importance of having a wider engagement strategy to shore up our country's resilience.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I would like to ask how is the Ministry deepening Singapore's engagement with other key partners beyond the ASEAN region?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I look forward to hearing from the Ministry the new efforts and measures they will put in place to sustain the relationship and engagement that has been built over the years for the present and the future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, due to the pandemic travel restrictions, many Singaporean Muslims have not been able to perform the Haj and the Umrah since last year.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Saudi government also limited the number of Haj pilgrims and only to residents within Saudi Arabia last year.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How is the Ministry working with the Saudi Arabian authorities to ensure our citizens have opportunities to perform their pilgrimage safely when restrictions are lifted?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Minister advise when Singaporean Muslims can look forward to making their annual pilgrimages?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would their vaccination status, for example, have any impact on their opportunities for them to do so?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, amid the closing of borders and lockdowns, and the gloom due to the pandemic, paradoxically, the Middle East has shown some promise of peace in the region last one year.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In another new chapter in the region, Saudi Arabia and three other Arab countries have reinstated diplomatic relations with Qatar – three years after ties were cut with Doha.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These agreements would perhaps signal a major shift in Middle Eastern geopolitics, which have long been characterised by the refusal of Gulf Arab states to engage in talks with Israel.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The agreement can perhaps motivate additional Arab nations to negotiate bilaterally to normalise relationships with Israel.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There are, of course, others who feel that the agreement would again ignore the most controversial regional issues such as the Palestinian question or the fraught relationship with Tehran.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore and the Middle East have always had high-level exchanges, economic cooperation and people-to-people linkages.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have also a good relationship with Israel and the Singapore-Israel Industrial Research and Development Foundation has been supporting joint industrial R&D projects between companies from both countries.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, while peace portents well for the world, we are reminded that the region is still very much a tinder box with the new US administration's tense new relationship with Saudi Arabia, continued acrimony with Iran and unease with some of the Israeli administration's policies.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Given these major developments in the Middle East, what are the implications for our foreign policy?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, trade is one of the most important pillars of our economy.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has impacted many of our established markets and it is timely for us to consider greater diversification.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should consider tapping into opportunities in other markets, especially those beyond Asia.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Emerging economies in central and eastern Europe, the Middle East and Latin America are developing strongly with young populations.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While they may not be obvious choices for our entrepreneurs, these are promising markets worth considering.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How are we engaging these emerging markets beyond Asia?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Minister provide an update on the measures and frameworks, such as trade agreements, to support Singapore companies there?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How else is the Ministry supporting local companies interested in exploring opportunities in these markets?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, in delivering Singapore's National Statement at the 74th Session of the United Nations General Assembly in 2019, the Prime Minister said, "For small countries like Singapore, multilateral institutions, systems and laws are critical for our survival.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: These give us a stake in the global commons and a means to defend and advance our interests.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: A rules-based system imposes responsibilities on all countries and creates a stable environment for all.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: This is why Singapore is a staunch advocate of the United Nations (UN), international law and of the multilateral system." For many decades, the United States has played the leadership role in forging a global multilateral system.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: However, the immediate past US President Donald Trump had very different views or rather, he had his own way to perform the role.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: On the environment front, there were nearly 100 rollbacks under the Trump administration to loosen regulations on everything from air and water quality to wildlife.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: In 2017, Trump announced his intention to withdraw from the Paris Agreement.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Mr Biden called climate change an existential threat to the health of our planet and to our very survival.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: He vowed to reverse some of the Trump administration's policies as well as enact more of his own to combat climate change.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: There is a Chinese saying, 朝更暮改, which literally means: what was just changed in the morning, changes again at night.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: However, it would be wrong to label the United States, a global superpower, as fickle in its policies.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Its institutions would be able to provide a good level of policy consistency from administration to administration.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: On the other hand, the United States has become more polarised as a nation.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: While Trump lost the elections, he still won more votes than any other presidential candidate, with the exception of Joe Biden.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: With such a domestic landscape, how does Singapore see political considerations shaping future policy developments in US international relations?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Can the Minister share how Singapore will seek to work with the new Biden administration?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Mr Chairman, last year, Singapore and China celebrated the 30th anniversary of the establishment of our diplomatic relations.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore's economy depends heavily on trade and China is Singapore's biggest trading partner.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is the highest level of bilateral platforms between both countries.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Connectivity, digitalisation and sustainable development are increasingly critical areas for collaboration in a post-COVID-19 world.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have to ensure that the Singapore-China economic relationship is mutually beneficial and not one which is a win-lose.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Does COVID-19 have an adverse impact on existing areas of cooperation?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What is the state of our relations with China and the progress of our government-to-government projects?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Mr Chairman, Singaporean businesses have internationalised well in the China market and with many great success stories.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is to a large extent due to the substantive and multi-faceted relations that the two countries have built and enjoyed over the decades.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Economic ties between the two countries are robust and continually being improved upon with regular enhancements to bilateral free trade agreements and new cooperation initiatives.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The series of government-to-government projects like the latest China-Singapore (Chongqing) Connectivity Initiative demonstrate strong state-level relations and have helped add further impetus to the economic relations at both the strategic and the business levels.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For Singaporean businesses, the annual Joint Council for Bilateral Cooperation (JCBC) meetings, co-chaired by the Deputy Prime Minister Heng and China's Vice Premier Han Zheng, are often highly anticipated events where businesses look out for announcements in new areas of cooperation or for better mutual accesses to each other's markets.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: China is a massive and diverse market, with each region and province offering varying business opportunities and investment potential.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is not possible for Singaporean businesses to be in every part of China.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It makes sense for Singaporean businesses to operate, where possible, in areas where we have consular and economic agencies' support.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I ask the Minister how would MFA shape Singapore-China relations in the new global landscape and what would be the new focuses in the area of economic, trade and investment relations?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: What opportunities are there for Singaporean businesses in China, especially at the provincial and at the city levels?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For these Singaporeans, the MFA's Overseas Mission serves as the primary point of contact when they require any assistance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: COVID-19 has placed some of these Singaporeans in a precarious state, especially for those in countries where the virus is less well-contained.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many of them would still be unable to return to Singapore for work or health reasons.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: COVID-19 has accentuated the need for Overseas Missions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the MFA provide an update on how it has provided consular assistance to Singaporeans abroad during the COVID-19 pandemic?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What roles do MFA's Overseas Missions play in providing consular assistance and what should Singaporeans in need of such assistance do?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What challenges does MFA face that require the public's support?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, the strategic balance in the world is shifting due to the tussle between the United States and China.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The world powers are going through a complex adaption to the new world order.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Regional blocs and smaller countries have to similarly find its place in the new system.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic's impact on critical food, medical supplies and vaccines are a good example of how complex international relations can have acute impact on Singapore's survivability in the longer run.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Against the backdrop of a more participative and cosmopolitan citizenry and international relations frequently being played out on social media, can the MFA share how it has engaged with Singaporeans on our foreign policy and how fellow Singaporeans can play their part in it?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can the Ministry better share complex foreign policies regularly so that Singaporeans can better understand our bilateral and multilateral initiatives?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore had flourished, despite our lack of natural resources, by being attuned to the needs of our region and the world.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: By fulfilling these needs and adding value, we had aligned the interests of our allies with our own and had thus been able to earn our place in the world.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our relevance had enabled us to survive and thrive.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has led to many disruptions and changes.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, ever improving online connectivity has shrunk distances between nations, bypassed physical obstacles and blunted certain geographical advantages.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To stay relevant within this new order, we will have to change course, invest more in certain sectors and partnerships, reduce resource allocations for others or even give up certain endeavours.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Ministry share how Singapore is working to retain its relevance internationally in this challenging environment?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How can we remake ourselves so that we remain a valued member in the international community?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the face of weakening multilateralism, what is Singapore's strategy to secure our place amidst international engagements?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A cornerstone of Singapore's foreign policies defending our interest at multilateral organisations, such as the International Civil Aviation Organization and International Maritime Organization.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore has won a seat on the councils of both organisations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Towards securing our candidatures, we need to depend on the support of more than just our major and regional partners.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore also has to engage countries in Africa, Latin America, the Carribean and the Pacific Islands.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, engaging these countries is a mammoth task.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Inevitably, we sacrifice depth of knowledge for width of engagement.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can I ask the Minister, are the current resources sufficient, given increased competition from other countries?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, is MFA receiving enough support from other Government agencies?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While it is understandable that domestic issues are prioritised over hosting foreign visitors, sharing expertise and offering technical assistance, the latter set of actions are a key aspect of our engagement in our larger foreign policy goals.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am glad that the Singapore Cooperation Programme (SCP) has moved some courses online.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The SCP is a useful tool in building goodwill for Singapore and it is vital that its effectiveness is maintained despite COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The on-going pandemic has reduced the number of opportunities for direct high-level physical contacts with these countries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Has MFA been able to maintain or step up such contacts through virtual meetings?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Sitting on the coffee table at my firm's lobby is a book titled "The Singapore Foreign Service: The First 40 Years".

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I received this as a young Foreign Service Officer in my first job.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I placed it at my lobby so that visitors can peruse it while waiting for their meetings or interviews and in a small way, help to educate people on the important work that our foreign service does.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I recall then-Foreign Minister George Yeo, not long after the launch of this book in 2006, saying in this House that our Foreign Service Officers (FSOs) are a "special group of people".

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, while we are safely cloistered here at home, largely unaffected by the pandemic, let us remember that there are fellow Singaporeans overseas, doing their part at the absolute frontlines of this battle against COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: On this note, I would like to echo Member Henry Kwek in thanking all of our Foreign Service Officers and diplomatic staff overseas for their dedication, courage, loyalty and service to Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 2.55 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 2.34 pm until 2.55 pm.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Chairman, when I spoke at last year's Committee of Supply (COS), at that point in time we had just repatriated 266 people from Wuhan, our own citizens.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And this just in the initial days of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, 2020 has been a very busy year.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: There were many challenges, but we were determined to leave no Singaporean behind.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Around the world, flights were disrupted, borders were closed, public health situations were deteriorating.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And we had an unprecedented number of requests for consular assistance.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In some countries like India, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, we were able to mount repatriation flights to bring large groups home.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But there were other places where Singaporeans were stuck in areas where we had no ground presence, no embassies.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I am glad that members of this House have conveyed their appreciation to the men and women of MFA, all of whom, I want to emphasise, have remained unflinchingly at post overseas throughout this crisis, even as it worsened.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Many of them are still separated from their family members, after one year.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: More than 300 of our officers continue serving at our overseas missions.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: They fly our flag abroad, keep in touch with Singaporeans overseas, help those who wish to come home, provide support to those who choose to remain.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: They also work closely with our economic and health agencies to sustain our flows of food, medical supplies and vaccines.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: They are part of the whole-of-Government of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I should also say, although I will not reveal the numbers, that some of our MFA officers have been infected with COVID-19 whilst they were overseas at post.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: For privacy reasons and operational reasons, I hope you will not ask me for the numbers, But let me assure this House that fortunately, all of them have recovered and are well.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But again, this reflects our debt to them.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Their grit and their resilience and their commitment to duty in the face of a crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our Foreign Service Officers have worked over many years to build up diplomatic capital and in the last one year, we have drawn down on this capital.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: For example, where we had no embassies, we reached out to our partners including Malaysia, Japan, France, the UK, Israel and Taiwan to help bring our people home.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Similarly, where we could, we also facilitated the return and transits of other countries’ nationals using our aircraft or transiting through Changi Airport.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Alex Yam had also asked about how we helped to ensure supply chain connectivity.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In the early days of the crisis, when borders were closing, we worked with partners like Australia, Canada, Chile, New Zealand and our fellow ASEAN countries to keep the supplies of essential goods flowing.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Efforts over the years to enhance our presence at multilateral fora have also paid off.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have participated actively at the UN, at the WHO and the WTO.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And our networks were also key to securing our vaccine supplies early and to minimise delays.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But beyond shoring up our foundation in a time of crisis, we are also building up resilience for a post-COVID-19 future.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In this shifting, uncertain and volatile environment, strengthening our resilience is inextricably intertwined with increasing our relevance to the world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Lee Kuan Yew's reminder to us to always seek relevance, has never rung more true than today.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: COVID-19 amplified the push for shorter supply chains, for greater efficiency and security, and many countries were stampeded into this.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It reaffirmed the role of free trade for shared prosperity and peace.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Both the RCEP and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, or CPTPP, remain open, the door remains open for like-minded economies to join, and as pathfinders to what we hope will ultimately be even wider agreements.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: For Singapore, I do not think I need to remind the House that trade remains three times our GDP.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, this is not a debating point, trade is our lifeblood.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Sustaining international support for trade helps bolster our economic growth, as well as create jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Second priority, to enhance our nexus for trade, shipping, finance, and data, and even more important, ideas.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Throughout this crisis, Singapore has continued to be a transit hub for foreign nationals who needed desperately to get home, as well as for crew changes for the maritime industry so that essential supplies and food, and medication can continue to move across the globe.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is one reason why MOT has been very busy.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is the other reason why, you will continue to see from time to time, we will have cases, apparently imported.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Because, unlike other countries, complete isolation and shut down is not a viable strategy for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Although, Members of the House will also appreciate that green lanes' bubbles will have to open and shut according to circumstances.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But the more important point is that we have continued to be a paragon of reliability, trustworthiness, that we have honoured at all times, the sanctity of contracts.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have never impounded supplies even when the crisis was deep.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The third priority is to promote multi-stakeholder partnerships.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: COVID-19 has in fact shown that we can achieve new levels of partnership between government, civil society and industry – across borders – when we are united around a common purpose.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: For example, we have seen unprecedented levels of international scientific and medical cooperation throughout this crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: China scientists actually published the genome of the SARS-CoV-2 virus in January last year.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Because they published it and because Singapore also played a small but important role in curating and processing the genome – and in fact, subsequent massive amounts of data on the genome database for COVID-19 – diagnostic tests were quickly developed all over the world, including in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: There has been effective cooperation across borders to share research and to develop tests, vaccines and treatments.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling asked how Singapore has contributed to international efforts to fight COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Apart from our work on diagnostic kits, we were also amongst the first in the world to launch digital contact tracing solutions and one of the first to develop a contact tracing protocol, which we then open-sourced so others could access it, use it, modify it.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We must start with the principle, that fair and equitable access to vaccines across the globe is essential.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is not an ideological position, this is a practical proposition, because no one is safe, until everyone is safe.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is especially so for a small, open country like Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We founded and we co-chair the Friends of the COVAX Facility group, to provide impetus and support for the Facility's development.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is very easy now to say, "Oh, that's obvious.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Why don't you do more?" But we will put our hands up when it was not obvious and when everyone was focused internally.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, on this count, Singapore is a net donor.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Now, in a panic, in a crisis, it is actually quite natural for every country to look to secure supplies for themselves first.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But we know that the virus knows no borders.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: COVAX's primary value is in supporting wider access to vaccines.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Without it, we would all be collectively worse off.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In fact, Members may or may not be aware that it was Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong who introduced the term "vaccine multilateralism", which everyone bandies about now.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our quantum took into account the needs of the larger international community, and also our status as a tiny city state, but a responsible and contributing member of the international community.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The need for a multilateral approach to fight COVID-19 is therefore, self-evident.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This virus, I repeat, does not discriminate across language, race, religion or borders.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And therefore, it is in our collective interest to help each other.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The fourth priority is climate change and many Members have referred to this.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I am pleased to report that even in the midst of the pandemic, many countries continued to push ahead with implementing their obligations under the Paris Agreement.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: China, South Korea and Japan announced net zero targets.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And we welcome the return of the US to the Paris Agreement.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: As a small island state, Singapore is disproportionately affected by climate change, but this is not a problem we can solve on our own.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We must continue to work with the international community to operationalise, in a real and practical way, the Paris Agreement.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: For Singapore, MFA will work with other Ministries to do our part as a responsible member of the international community.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We will seek new areas of cooperation, in innovating to build greener, more liveable cities, and because the world has now reached the point where more than half of humanity live in cities, urban solutions that we generate in Singapore will have salience and will be relevant all over the world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Therefore, we will help sustain global momentum towards a more sustainable future.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This brings me to the fifth area, digital cooperation, which Mr Henry Kwek addressed.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The digital revolution was actually well under way before the onset of COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The pandemic actually acted as a stress test, it was a catalyst, it sped up our movement online, voluntarily or otherwise; and everyone had to rely on digital tools for work, for school, for purchases, for transactions.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: At home and abroad, we are also supporting capacity-building.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng put a lot into education and skills and training, and that is to make sure that Singaporeans will have the skills and the capacity to be at the forefront of this global revolution.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: At the UN, ASEAN and other platforms, we will continue to work with our partners to develop and strengthen norms of responsible state behaviour in cyberspace.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Here you know I am referring to cybersecurity, which, in fact, remains a clear and present danger for all of us.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Even more so now, that we are so dependent on digital technologies.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Making progress on these priorities that I have just outlined, will not be easy.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The world will continue to feel the pandemic's after-effects for several years to come.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: There will still be great geopolitical and macroeconomic risk for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I want to spend some time addressing this question of "risk to Singapore".

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Governments have rolled out fiscal measures, loosened monetary measures, corporations have borrowed to stay afloat during the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In the short term, these steps have helped to avert the worst economic consequences for the globe.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But you know these are ultimately not sustainable in the long run.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: That means, managing the transition will be a perilous journey for all of us, and especially for Singapore because of the role that we play in the global economy.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The second is that the economic impact of COVID-19 has deepened fault lines, all across the globe and led to divisions both within and between countries and societies.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Politically, that is why we are witnessing growing friction and distrust rather than cooperation and confidence-building.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: There has been increased pressure for governments to take a nationalistic, protectionist and isolationist approach.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have already seen this happen, whether it is the scramble for masks or PPE, or even now, in the distribution of vaccines.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Over the past year, we have witnessed sharp exchanges between senior figures on both sides.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The US-China relationship remains the linchpin for geopolitical stability.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But the fundamental shift in relations between two superpowers preceded the outbreak of COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: China is increasing its influence, asserting its place in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The younger generation in China who grown up in the last 40 years have only known ascendency and they will not tolerate being treated or even perceive being treated unfairly by any foreign power.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: At the same time – and I tell you as a person who has had to travel frequently to the United States over the past five years, except for last year –now there is absolutely no doubt that there bipartisan support in the US for a tougher stance against China, to rectify what they believe are unfair practices, trade practices as well as to deal with a contest, a competition with a strategic rival on a scale that United States has never faced before.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Friction over trade, emerging technologies, human rights, defence, finance and cybersecurity have all continued unabated.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But I still believe, or perhaps you can say that it is a hope, that the US and China will find ways to manage their relations.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Practical cooperation is possible, especially if it is conducted within a rules-based multilateral system, with established rules and norms of engagement.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Some areas, in fact, COVID-19 is an example, which has starkly reminded the world of our interdependence and it would have been far more effective if the US and China had been able to cooperate effectively from day one.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Another area where you need effective cooperation between the two superpowers is climate change.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In 2015, as a Ministerial facilitator for the negotiations that ultimately led to the Paris Agreement, I witnessed first-hand how effective cooperation between the US and China enabled us to achieve what would otherwise have been unattainable in 2015.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: President Biden and President Xi had their first official phone call recently – I am sure it was carefully selected – the date was on the eve of Chinese New Year.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: They spoke about their respective concerns and differences.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But they also discussed tackling COVID-19, the global health system, climate change and countering proliferation.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I think that is a good start but without wishing away all the fundamental hurdles, obstacles and prickliness to their relationship.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In our own region, it will be crucial to maintain ASEAN Centrality amidst this greater geopolitical competition and uncertainty.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We must continue strengthening ASEAN integration in concrete ways, whether in public health, economic cooperation or establishing protocols to prepare for safe re-opening.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And this will reinforce the concentric circles of an open and inclusive regional architecture, which includes mechanisms like the East Asia Summit and the ASEAN Regional Forum and help ASEAN hold together, even as external forces try to push us or pull us one way or another, as it will invariably happen.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And Myanmar, unfortunately, is a case in point.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The recent developments in Myanmar are a source of grave concern to Singapore and indeed, to the larger ASEAN family.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Yesterday, I think you all know there was a significant escalation in violence across the cities in Myanmar.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Security forces shot at civilians with live rounds, rubber bullets, stun grenades and tear gas.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are appalled by the use of lethal force against civilians.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We express our heartfelt condolences to the families of those who have lost their lives and we hope that the injured will recover quickly.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Prolonged instability in Myanmar will have serious consequences for Myanmar, for ASEAN and across our region.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Despite ASEAN's core principles of consensus and non-interference, ASEAN can still play a constructive role in facilitating, hopefully, a return to normalcy and stability in Myanmar.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This was why Singapore strongly supported ASEAN's efforts from the start, including the ASEAN Chair's Statement.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We believe in engagement and dialogue in good faith with all relevant stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: ASEAN will also work closely with all our external partners to foster an inclusive dialogue with all key stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And we must ensure that the mutually beneficial relations that ASEAN and our partners have built up do not become paralysed by this issue.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: If we can hold together and maintain ASEAN Centrality, the longer term prospects for our region are still robust.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In case people do not appreciate the use of the word "centrality", it is not just jargon.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: You see, the choice for Southeast Asia is either we hang together, as what Mr Rajaratnam said at our founding, or for us to become fragmented into battleground and proxy states and vessel states.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, when we say "centrality" and "integration", these are crucial for all the 10 members of Southeast Asia, all the more so when there is geopolitical instability.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But if we can hold together, hang together, maintain centrality, then our longer term prospects for our region, in fact, are bright.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
